To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hard seeds are an effective strategy to avoid predation by rodents and to promote rodent seed-dispersal.

hard-seededness can evolve as a predator-escape mechanism, and that optimal seed dispersal and survival success in the presence of rodent seed predators are obtained by plants having dimorphic soft and rodent dispersed hard seeds.

water impermeable seed coats reduce seed predation in the absence of dormancy functions and that the optimal seed survival in environments with rodent predators is obtained by having dimorphic soft and impermeable hard seed strategies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ecological functions of hard seeds and the evolutionary forces that have shaped the evolution of seed dimorphism.
the ecological and evolutionary mechanisms underlying the evolution of hard seeds and the evolution of dimorphic soft and ‘hard’ seeds.
how the evolution of plant traits is affected by the ecology of the organisms interacting with them, and how the evolution of these organisms is affected by the traits of plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hard seeds are a dispersal and predation strategy, rather than a dormancy strategy.
hard seeds can be a dispersal and a predator escape strategy, and that the primary function of hard seeds is not dormancy, but predator avoidance.
hard seeds are not dormant, but that hard seeds are produced by plants as a strategy to reduce seed predations and to promote rodent seed-dispersal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hard-seededness is a strategy to reduce seed predations, and that it may be a by-product of the evolution of seed dormancy.
hard seeds are not only a dormancy trait, but also a predator avoidance trait.
the evolution and ecology of water-impermeability in seeds is more complex than previously assumed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of hard seeds may be driven by the need to escape from seed predators, rather than by dormancy requirements.
the crypsis and dormancy hypotheses of hard seeds may not be mutually exclusive.
seed survival success can be maximised by producing dimorphic soft (dispersible) and hard (predator escape) seeds.
